   Guide to City Council Proceedings

Meetings of the City Council are held the first and third Tuesday of each month at 9:00 a.m. and are
conducted in accordance with Rosenberg's Rules of Order (Vernon Municipal Code Section
2.04.020).

Copies of all agenda items and back-up materials are available for review in the City Clerk
Department, Vernon City Hall, 4305 Santa Fe Avenue, Vernon, California, and are available for
public inspection during regular business hours, Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.
Agenda reports may be reviewed on the City's website at www.cityofvernonca.gov or copies may be
purchased for $0.20 per page.

Disability-related services are available to enable persons with a disability to participate in this
meeting, consistent with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). In compliance with ADA, if you
need special assistance, please contact the City Clerk department at CityClerk@cityofvernonca.gov
or (323) 583-8811 at least 48 hours prior to the meeting to assure arrangements can be made.

The Public Comment portion of the agenda is for members of the public to present items, which are
not listed on the agenda but are within the subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council. The City
Council cannot take action on any item that is not on the agenda but matters raised under Public
Comment may be referred to staff or scheduled on a future agenda. Comments are limited to three
minutes per speaker unless a different time limit is announced. Speaker slips are available at the
entrance to the Council Chamber.

Public Hearings are legally noticed hearings. For hearings involving zoning matters, the applicant
and appellant will be given 15 minutes to present their position to the City Council. Time may be set
aside for rebuttal. All other testimony shall follow the rules as set for under Public Comment. If you
challenge any City action in court, you may be limited to raising only those issues you or someone
else raised during the public hearing, or in written correspondence delivered to the City Clerk at or
prior to the public hearing.

Consent Calendar items may be approved by a single motion. If a Council Member or the public
wishes to discuss an item, it may be removed from the calendar for individual consideration. Council
Members may indicate a negative or abstaining vote on any individual item by so declaring prior to
the vote on the motion to adopt the Consent Calendar. Items excluded from the Consent Calendar
will be taken up following action on the Consent Calendar. Public speakers shall follow the
guidelines as set forth under Public Comment.

New Business items are matters appearing before the Council for the first time for formal action.
Those wishing to address the Council on New Business items shall follow the guidelines for Public
Comment.

Closed Session allows the Council to discuss specific matters pursuant to the Brown Act,
Government Code Section 54956.9. Based on the advice of the City Attorney, discussion of these
matters in open session would prejudice the position of the City. Following Closed Session, the City
Attorney will provide an oral report on any reportable matters discussed and actions taken. At the
conclusion of Closed Session, the Council may continue any item listed on the Closed Session
agenda to the Open Session agenda for discussion or to take formal action as it deems appropriate.

Meeting Date:  March 17, 2026
From:  Brian Saeki, City Administrator
Department:  City Administration
Submitted by:  Brian Saeki, City Administrator

Subject
City Council Strategic Priorities

Recommendation
Receive a presentation on potential City Council goals and determine key goals to guide the
City’s strategic planning process.

Background
As directed by the City Council, the City engaged Kelly Associates Management Group to assist
with a goal-setting process, a priority for the Council as it shapes Vernon’s path forward.

The process began with the preparation of a SWOT analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses,
Opportunities, and Threats), which was shared with the City Council, executive and other staff,
and community stakeholders, including the Chamber of Commerce. In addition, interviews were
conducted with these same stakeholders.

The City also hosted three community meetings to gather input from residents and businesses.
Resident meetings were held in the evening on February 2, 2026, at the Vernon Village
Apartments and on February 5, 2026, in the City Council Chambers at City Hall. A business
breakfast at City Hall was held that same morning on February 5th.

Responses from the SWOT analysis and feedback from the community meetings were compiled,
summarized, and presented to the City Council at a special meeting on March 3, 2026. During
the meeting, the City Council was asked to help identify approximately five key goals by placing
red dots on the items considered most important. Each Council Member was limited to five dots
to ensure the goals selected remained manageable. While Council Members acknowledged that
more than five goals were important, the need to narrow the list for focused action was
understood.

The City Council placed their dots on the following priorities:

Three Dots:
  • Proactively engage in economic development and planning for the City’s future
  • Develop community facilities (park/community center, dog park, library, health clinic)
  • Enhanced long-term financial and capital planning

Two Dots:
  • Review public safety alternatives
  • Reduce environmental impacts in Southeast Los Angeles Area (SELA) communities
  • Actively pursue residential and retail development
  • Green tech and circular economy, position the city to become a clean-tech hub

One. Dot:
  .

   •  Continue to build credibility among other public agencies and the public
  •  Seek new/increased funding (tax revenues, state/federal allocations, creative partnership
  opportunities
  •  Improve local air quality and sell power
  •  Streamline and refine the City’s code, purchasing policy and procedures
  •  Provide services to surrounding cities to generate revenue
  •  Digital infrastructure (data centers)
  •  Kern County property
  •  OE Clark Community Center

No other goals were marked by dots.

Discussion
Based on the priorities identified by the City Council, staff have developed the following six (6)
potential goals for Council consideration:

  1. Strengthen City Credibility and Partnerships
  •  Build trust and credibility with the public and other public agencies
  •  Pursue collaborative opportunities with regional partners to maximize impact
  and resources
  2. Promote Economic Growth and Revenue Generation
  •  Attract residential, retail, and commercial development
  •  Provide services to surrounding cities and explore new revenue sources,
  including green tech and digital infrastructure investments
  3. Advance Sustainability and Environmental Stewardship
  •  Improve local air quality and reduce environmental impacts, particularly in SELA
  communities
  •  Position Vernon as a hub for clean-tech and circular economy initiatives
  4. Enhance Community Infrastructure and Facilities
  •  Develop parks, community centers (including OE Clark building), libraries, and
  health clinics to meet resident needs
  •  Invest in digital and physical infrastructure that supports both community and
  economic goals
  •  Explore new funding mechanisms to finance public infrastructure and
  development projects (e.g. Enhanced Infrastructure Financing District (EIFD))
  5. Strengthen Organizational Efficiency and Financial Planning
  •  Streamline City codes, policies, and procedures, including purchasing
  processes
  •  Streamline City meetings to enhance public engagement and efficiency
  •  Implement long-term financial and capital planning to ensure sustainability and
  resilience
  6. Optimize Public Utility Operations to Ensure Affordable Services
  •  Prioritize the efficient management of the City’s power, gas, fiber, and water
  systems
  •  Keep utility costs low for residents and businesses while maintaining reliable,
  high-quality service
  •  Kern County property

These goals are recommendations for the City Council to consider. They may be added to or
  .
amended during the presentation to the City Council. Additionally, the Strategic Plan is a living
  .

 document that may be modified at any time as new priorities arise. The plan will also be formally
evaluated each year, typically during the budget process for the following fiscal year.

Once the goals are set and approved by the City Council, staff will develop specific tasks to help
achieve them. Each task will include a schedule, any associated costs, and the responsible City
department.

Fiscal Impact
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report.

Meeting Date:  March 17, 2026
From:  Daniel S. Wall, P.E., Director of Public Works-City Engineer
Department:  Public Works
Submitted by:  Rosemary Lozada, Management Analyst

Subject
Adoption of the 2025 California Building Standards Code by Reference

Recommendation
A. Conduct a Public Hearing;
B. Find that the proposed action is exempt from California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
review, because it is general policy and procedure-making activity that is unrelated to any
specific project, which must undergo separate CEQA review, and that will not result in direct
physical changes or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical changes in the environment, and
therefore does not constitute a “project” as defined by CEQA Guidelines Section 15378; and
C. Adopt Ordinance No. 1310 adopting the 2025 California Building Standards Code by
reference.

Background
During the regular City Council Meeting on March 3, 2026, the City Council introduced and
conducted the first reading of Ordinance No. 1310 adopting the 2025 California Building
Standards Code. This ordinance adopts the 2025 California Building Standards Code by
reference. Every three years, the California Department of General Services' Building Code
Standards Commission reviews, revises and adopts building and construction codes. These
building codes are comprehensive standards used by the design and construction community
and relied upon by the insurance industry to minimize the loss of life and property.

Pursuant to California Government Code Sections 50022.2, 50022.3 and 6066, the public
hearing notice was published on February 26 and March 5, 2026. The public hearing will be held
on March 17, 2026, prior to the adoption of Ordinance No. 1310.

Fiscal Impact
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report.

2. Notice of Public Hearing

Subject
Sidewalk Vending Regulations

Recommendation
A. Conduct a Public Hearing;
B. Find that the proposed action is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15061(b)(3) and 15378, as an action for which there is
no possibility that the ordinance will have any significant effect on the environment;
C. Introduce, read by title only, and waive further reading of Ordinance No. 1311 amending
Chapter 12.10 (Sidewalk Vending) of Title 12 (Streets, Sidewalks and Public Places) of the
Vernon Municipal Code pertaining to the regulation of sidewalk vending; and
D. Direct staff to schedule the adoption for the April 7, 2026, City Council meeting.

Background
On February 15, 2022, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. 1276, which established Chapter
12.10 of the Vernon Municipal Code (VMC) to regulate sidewalk vending in accordance with state
mandates. Since then, the California State Legislature has further refined the scope of local
authority for permitting and enforcing these activities.

Effective January 1, 2026, California Senate Bill 635 (SB 635) provides revised guidance for local
agencies regarding the management of sidewalk vending applications and vendor data.
Salient points in Ordinance No. 1311 pursuant to SB 635:

  •  Prohibition of Background Checks: Local agencies are now prohibited from requiring
  fingerprinting or criminal background checks as a condition for receiving or renewing a
  sidewalk vending permit.
  •  Immigration Status Protections: The law prohibits cities from inquiring about or collecting
  any information regarding an applicant’s citizenship or immigration status.
  •  Data Privacy and Disclosure: SB 635 restricts the disclosure of personally identifiable
  information to third parties or other governmental agencies. Such information can only be
  released if required by a judicial warrant or a subpoena.

This ordinance aligns the VMC with the mandates of SB 635 by 1) removing the requirement for
annual fingerprinting and background checks previously found in VMC Section 12.10.030, 2)
further updating definitions to ensure clear legal boundaries, and 3) including determination
clauses and specific enforcement restrictions.

A public hearing notice was published on March 5, 2026 for the public hearing on March 17,
2026.

Staff recommends that, on March 17, 2026, the City Council introduce and read the proposed
ordinance

Section 12.10.010. Purpose.

Sidewalk vending promotes entrepreneurship and can provide a vibrant street scene. The
procedures and standards in this article are intended to provide an orderly framework
allowing street vending while protecting the health and wellbeing of the public.

Section 12.10.020. Definitions.

“Immigration enforcement” means “immigration enforcement” as that term is defined in

or assist in the investigation or enforcement of any state or federal civil immigration law,

or enforcement of any state or federal criminal immigration law that penalizes a person’s

number, consular identification, social media identifiers, employer identification number,
business license number, seller’s permit number, social security number, vending
registration certificate or license number, known place of work, income and tax
information, and any other information that would identify the individual.

Section 12.10.040. General regulations.

(A) To maintain accessibility standards for the disabled, every sidewalk vendor operating
  on any public street or right-of-way must ensure that no obstruction is placed in the
  public street or right-of-way that would reduce the width of the public street or right-
  of-way to less than forty-eight (48) inches, exclusive of the top of the curb. No
  obstruction shall be located in a public street or right-of-way less than six (6) feet in
  width when the sidewalk is adjacent to the curb.

(B) To prevent food-borne illness and protect the health and safety of the City's residents,
  every sidewalk vendor selling any food or beverage is required to adhere to the
  provisions of California Health and Safety Code, Division 104 (Environmental
  Health), Part 7 (California Retail Food Code).

(C) A sidewalk vending permit does not provide an exclusive right to operate within any
  specific portion of the public street or right-of-way.

(D) No equipment or objects used for sidewalk vending purposes may be left unattended
  in public spaces or in any portion of the public street or right-of-way from 10:00 p.m.
  to 6:00 a.m. Any equipment or objects left overnight in public spaces or in any portion
  of the public street or right-of-way will be considered discarded and may be seized
  or disposed of by the City in accordance with this article.

(E) To facilitate the enforcement of this article, every sidewalk vendor must display their
  city-issued sidewalk vending permit on the street-side portion of their sidewalk
  vending receptacle when operating in the public street or right-of-way.

(F) To preserve accessibility to private and public facilities, a sidewalk vendor operating
  on any public street or right-of-way must ensure that no obstruction is placed
  impeding entry to and exit from a business or residence or access to a public facility.

(G) A sidewalk vendor shall not engage in the selling of alcohol, cannabis, tobacco
  products, products that contain nicotine or any product used to smoke/vape nicotine
  or cannabis, or adult-oriented material depicting, describing or relating to sexual
  activities.

(H) A sidewalk vendor must carry a waste disposal bag or container to permit the
  disposal of trash, food, or liquids.

(I)  No sidewalk vending receptacle shall contain or use propane, natural gas, or other
  explosive or hazardous materials. A sidewalk vendor may not use an open flame on
  or within any sidewalk vending receptacle.

(J) Sidewalk vending receptacles shall not touch, lean against, or be affixed at any time
  to any building or structure including, but not limited to lampposts, parking meters,

Section 12.10.050. Location-specific regulations.

(A) Sidewalk vending hours' limitations in areas zoned for nonresidential use will be as

(D) A sidewalk vendor is prohibited from operating within five hundred (500) feet of any

(E) To limit traffic congestion and protect the safety of children traveling to and from and
  in and around schools from potential adverse safety impacts due, in part, to sidewalk

(F) To limit traffic congestion and protect the safety of transit riders from potential

  second violation; or

   NOTICE OF CITY COUNCIL PUBLIC HEARING
The City Council of the City of Vernon will conduct a public hearing on March 17, 2026, at
9:00 a.m. (or as soon thereafter as the matter can be heard) which you may attend at Vernon
City Hall, City Council Chamber, 4305 Santa Fe Avenue, Vernon, CA 90058 to:

  ADOPT AN ORDINANCE AMENDING CHAPTER 12.10 (SIDEWALK
  VENDING) OF TITLE 12 (STREETS, SIDEWALKS AND PUBLIC
  PLACES) OF THE VERNON MUNICIPAL CODE REGULATING
  SIDEWALK VENDING

The proposed ordinance would amend Chapter 12.10 of the Vernon Municipal Code to
comply with new state law, SB 635 – the Street Vendor Business Protection Act, effective
January 1, 2026, which imposes limitations on local authorities regarding enforcement
and how data regarding sidewalk vending can be collected, stored, and shared. Key
amendments to the chapter include:

  •  In compliance with SB 635, amending the City’s sidewalk vending permitting
  process to remove fingerprinting and background check requirements;
  •  Updating enforcement procedures to comply with applicable state law, including
  prohibiting the use of City funds or personnel to engage in specified activities
  related to immigration enforcement when enforcing provisions regulating sidewalk
  vendors.

All relevant documents will be available for public review on the City’s website once the
agenda for the meeting is posted or from the City Clerk at cityclerk@cityofvernonca.gov
or (323) 583-8811, ext. 546. All interested persons will be given an opportunity to
comment on the above-referenced items during the public hearing. In addition, written
comment or questions may be submitted prior to the hearing as set forth below. Written
Testimony or questions must be received prior to 9:00 a.m. on the date of the hearing.

Please send your comments or questions to:

  and technical nature of the energy plan, her support for the City’s continued
  partnership with SCPPA. She expressed her preference for providing more time
  for public review and raised concerns about the 30-year term. She stated that the
  Chamber supports the plan's outlined savings. However, the Chamber does not

  recommended that the City hold future workshops for both the Council and the

   City Council Agenda Report

Meeting Date:  March 17, 2026
From:  Brian Saeki, City Administrator
Department:  City Administration
Submitted by:  Lilia Hernandez, Assistant to the City Administrator

Subject
Professional Services Agreement with Actum-E, LLC

Recommendation
A. Find that it is in the best interests of the City to award a contract directly to Actum-E, LLC
without a competitive selection process, pursuant to Vernon Municipal Code Section
3.32.110(B)(2); and
B. Approve and authorize the City Administrator to execute a Professional Services Agreement
with Actum-E, LLC, in substantially the same form as submitted, for government affairs related
to the Big 4 cities, for a total amount not-to-exceed $45,000, through June 30, 2026.

Background
On September 16, 2025, the City Council approved a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU)
with the cities of Commerce, Irwindale, Santa Fe Springs, Industry, and Vernon for the purpose
of uniting efforts to advocate for, advance, and plan shared priorities to seek state and federal
funding, and advocate for and advance legislative and administrative policies that address the
unique needs and benefits that their industrial and commercial activities offer Los Angeles County
and the State of California. Since, the cities of Commerce, Santa Fe Springs, and Industry have
executed the MOU along with Vernon and have initiated a plan for this multi-jurisdictional coalition
of “The Big 4” cities.

The Big 4 agreed to utilize the services of Actum-E, LLC (Actum) to assist with government affairs
and advocacy. Actum has substantial experience in these areas and will be instrumental in
advancing the Big 4’s collective goals. Actum’s priority is to assist the Big 4 in the pursuit of
legislative changes at the State level to increase SB1 (Road Repair and Accountability Act)
allocations for each of the respective Big 4 cities.

Utilizing one firm is most efficient and cost-effective, as it allows the four cities to share expenses.
Thus, contracting with Actum is in the best interests of the City pursuant to VMC Section
3.32.110(B)(2), as it optimizes the use of resources and minimizes costs. The agreement with
Actum provides the mechanism for the City to compensate Actum for Vernon’s ¼ share of costs
associated with the Big 4 efforts. The term of the agreement is retroactive to December 15, 2025
when Actum initiated work on behalf of the Big 4, and will continue through June 30, 2026. As
the Big 4 advance their shared interests, staff will reassess and determine if any services from
Actum will be needed in Fiscal Year (FY) 2025-26.

The proposed agreement with Actum-E, LLC requires City Council approval pursuant to Vernon
Municipal Code Section 3.32.030(B), as within the last 12 months, the City engaged this vendor
on a different matter, bringing the total combined amount paid or awarded to this vendor over
$100,000.

process, in accordance with City purchasing procedures and good governance contracting
principles.

The City Attorney’s Office estimates costs for outside legal services each fiscal year and seeks
contract approval or amendment consistent with budget allocations approved by City

2026-27, staff is requesting authority to enter into Amendment No. 1, which maintains all existing
terms under the current Agreement and increases the not-to-exceed amount by $75,000,
bringing the total contract amount to $150,000. Pursuant to Section 3.32.030(A) of the Vernon

of the contract exceeds $100,000. Amendment No. 1 has been reviewed and approved as to
form by the City Attorney.

Subject
Side Letters of Agreement with Police Bargaining Groups Regarding In-Lieu Holiday Time

Recommendation
A. Adopt Resolution No. 2026-011 approving the In-Lieu Holiday Time Side Letter of Agreement
by and between the City of Vernon and the Vernon Police Officers' Benefit Association (VPOBA);
and
B. Adopt Resolution No. 2026-012 approving the In-Lieu Holiday Time Side Letter of Agreement
by and between the City of Vernon and the Vernon Police Management Association (VPMA).

Background
The City recognizes two sworn police group associations which are Vernon Police Officers'
Benefit Association (VPOBA) and Vernon Police Management Association (VPMA). On
September 2, 2025, the City Council approved Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with these
bargaining groups for the term of July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2028.

Subsequent to MOU adoption, VPOBA employees requested VPOBA MOU language
clarification regarding In-Lieu Holiday Time. Following a thorough review, the City’s
Management team is recommending a revision to the In-Lieu Holiday Time language from City
observed holidays to City approved holidays and changes to the cash out eligibility to both the
VPOBA and VPMA MOUs. The VPOBA and VPMA bargaining groups are in agreement with the
proposed revisions to the In-Lieu Holiday Time and have agreed to execute Side Letters of
Agreement (Side Letters) to capture the changes.

Key changes to the In-Lieu Holiday Time language across both bargaining groups are as follows:
  • In-Lieu Holiday Time change from City observed holidays to City approved holidays
  effective July 1, 2025
  • Only allow In-Lieu Holiday Time cash out to VPMA or VPOBA employees who are off on
  Labor Code 4850 leave (temporarily disabled due to work-related injury)
  • Add Labor Code 4850 leave language to VPMA MOU

The proposed Side Letters and corresponding resolutions have been approved as to form by the
City Attorney.

Fiscal Impact
The fiscal impact will vary depending on staffing levels and operational scheduling needs when
the time is used. In-Lieu Holiday Time is not eligible for cash out except for employees on Labor
Code 4850 leave. Therefore, any fiscal impact is expected to be limited and absorbed within the
Police Department’s budget.

Subject
Removal of Marked Crosswalks Along Pacific Boulevard at 45th, 46th, and 49th Street

Recommendation
A. Find that the proposed action is categorically exempt from California Environmental Quality
Act (CEQA) review, in accordance with CEQA Guidelines Section 15301, because the project
consists of restriping an existing street by removing the crosswalk markings to avoid potential
adverse impacts to pedestrian and vehicular safety, and involves negligible or no expansion of
an existing use; and
B. Authorize pavement striping crew to remove all marked crosswalks along Pacific Boulevard at
45th, 46th, and 49th Street.

Background
The Public Works Department maintains a three-year traffic engineering consulting contract with
Albert Grover & Associates (AGA) to support the City’s ongoing efforts to enhance roadway
safety and operational efficiency. At the City’s request AGA conducted a comprehensive traffic
control evaluation at three intersections along Pacific Boulevard at 45th Street, 46th Street and
49th Street (Attachment 1).

City staff directed AGA the feasibility of installing pedestrian hybrid beacon traffic signal,
commonly referred to as High-Intensity Activated Crosswalk (HAWK) signals at these locations.
Each of these intersections currently includes ladder-style crosswalks across Pacific Boulevard,
a six-lane arterial with a posted speed limit of 40 mph. Pacific Boulevard carries significant heavy
freight traffic and automobile traffic, requiring a heightened level of scrutiny with respect to
pedestrian safety treatments.

The study determined that pedestrian crossing volumes at all three locations are exceptionally
low, with fewer than 20 pedestrians per hour observed. Based on these findings, AGA concluded
that the intersections do not meet the minimum thresholds established by the California Manual
on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) for installation of a HAWK signal, a full traffic signal,
or flashing yellow beacon warning devices. While the City retains discretion to apply engineering
judgment when considering traffic control measures, AGA’s analysis indicates that additional
pedestrian signalization at these locations is not warranted.

Given the minimal pedestrian demand at the intersections of Pacific Boulevard with 45th, 46th,
and 49th Streets, the Public Works Department has evaluated the appropriateness of retaining
the existing marked crosswalks. On wide, high-speed arterial roadways such as Pacific
Boulevard—particularly where parked or idling trucks frequently obstruct sight lines—marked
crosswalks may unintentionally create a false sense of security for pedestrians without providing
adequate protection from approaching vehicles. In the interest of improving overall pedestrian
safety, staff recommends consideration of removing the marked crosswalks at these locations.
Pedestrians would still be permitted to cross the roadway; however, the absence of marked
crosswalks is expected to encourage greater caution when doing so.

Pedestrian Hybrid Beacon (HAWK) Assessment Methodology

Each crosswalk was evaluated for a pedestrian hybrid beacon traffic control, also known as a HAWK
(High Intensity Activated Crosswalk). The HAWK is used to warn and control traffic to assist pedestrians
in crossing a crosswalk. The operation of a HAWK traffic signal is different than the typical traffic signal
(see Figure 2). When the HAWK indication is dark, vehicles may proceed through the crosswalk without
stopping. The HAWK will then flash yellow for a pedestrian call to signal for vehicles to slow down and
prepare to stop, then go to steady yellow prior to a steady red indication. As the pedestrian is crossing
the crosswalk during the WALK indication, the HAWK will have a steady red ball indicating that vehicles
should be at complete stop. Once the Flashing Don’t Walk (FDW) indication is on for the pedestrian,
the HAWK will have an alternating flashing red ball indicting that the vehicles may proceed through the
crosswalk if the pedestrian has cleared. The HAWK will then go back to dark until activated again.

  Figure 2: Sequence for a Pedestrian Hybrid Beacon

The benefit of utilizing a HAWK compared to a traffic signal is that vehicles can proceed through the
crosswalk once the pedestrian and/or bicyclists have safely cleared the crosswalk, even during the FDW
indication. While for a traffic signal, vehicles must wait for the entire pedestrian timing to be completed
before the proceeding which can cause unnecessary delays especially if a pedestrian or bicyclist has
crossed and cleared the crosswalk many seconds before the pedestrian timing has concluded. A HAWK
signal is less expensive than a full traffic signal since it involves less traffic signal equipment. The cost
of a HAWK signal could range from $250,000 - $350,000 compared to the cost of a full traffic signal
which could range from $500,000 to $750,000 depending on the configuration of the intersection.

One of the disadvantages of a HAWK is drivers may not be familiar with the traffic control device and
may not understand when they must stop and go during the dark phase. There has recently been an
increase in installation of HAWK traffic signals in Southern California. The City of Los Angeles has begun
installing HAWK traffic signals and plans to install additional HAWK traffic signals at various locations
throughout the City.

Other Traffic Control Devices

Other traffic control devices that are typically utilized at crosswalks are flashing yellow beacons
(including rapid rectangular flashing beacons – RRFB) and all-way stop controls. The flashing yellow
beacon is used to warn motorists of pedestrians crossing the street. The CA MUTCD has guidelines for
the application of the flashing yellow beacon at school crossings, but not for non-school areas. If any
of the studied traffic control devices (HAWK traffic signal and/or full traffic signal) are not warranted,
either traffic control device, including flashing yellow beacons, may still be implemented based on
engineering judgement and traffic conditions. The Rectangular Rapid-Flashing Beacon (RRFB) was not
assessed in this study as the FHWA does not recommend this traffic control for roadways with speeds
of 35mph or greater. In-roadway warning lights were also not assessed as these lights have specific
requirements for installation and operation, and maintaining these lights are very difficult, especially
areas with frequent truck traffic. For all three locations, stop control on the major streets was not
assessed as stop control is usually implemented for streets with lower traffic demand and when all
crossing streets have similar traffic volumes. For the study locations, the side street traffic volumes are
significantly less than the major street traffic volumes. Stop control on any of the major study streets
would significantly disrupt traffic conditions.

findings are similar to the previous intersections, a traffic signal is not warranted. The vehicle traffic

Street is less than 300 feet from the signalized intersection of Leonis Boulevard, installing traffic control
could disrupt traffic from and to Leonis Boulevard. The City could use engineering judgment to install
traffic control at this location. If traffic control is to be installed, it should be synchronized with the
intersection at Leonis Boulevard in order to not disrupt traffic along Pacific Boulevard.

Since there is a low number of pedestrians that cross Pacific Boulevard at 49th Street, there are
currently minimal disruptions to traffic on Pacific Boulevard. The City could also remove this crosswalk
and have pedestrians cross at Leonis Boulevard, which is a controlled crossing (traffic signal).

crossings at roadways where the speed limit exceeds 40 mph and the roadway has four or more lanes
with a minimum daily traffic of 12,000 vehicles per day. Even though the criteria do not apply to Pacific
Boulevard as the speed limit is 40 mph, pedestrian crossing warning signs could be installed at both the
advanced approaches and at the intersection, similar to 45th Street. The pedestrian crossing warning
signs are for only uncontrolled crosswalks and not associated with the HAWK traffic signal, full traffic

Conclusion

City staff had AGA conduct a Pedestrian Hybrid Beacon study to evaluate if the three intersections
qualify for a HAWK traffic signal, and also a traffic signal warrant study to determine if the intersections
qualify for a traffic signal. Traffic counts were conducted and the number of collisions were assessed.
The following summarized findings are provided:

  A) HAWK Traffic Signal - Based on the findings of Pedestrian Hybrid Beacon guidelines per the CA
  MUTCD, the pedestrian peak hour volumes did not meet the minimum threshold of 20
  pedestrians crossing the major street per hour. However, in studying 46th Street, it was found
  that this intersection had the highest pedestrian volume of 16 pedestrians during the
  pedestrian peak hour, which is close to the HAWK threshold of 20 pedestrians in an hour.
  Furthermore, It is important to note that this intersection also operates as a railroad crossing
  and has an existing railroad flashing light signal indications.

  B) Traffic Signal Warrant - Based on the findings of traffic signal warrant analysis, the traffic
  volumes did not meet the minimum thresholds for Warrant 1 (vehicle peak eight hours),
  Warrant 2 (vehicle peak four hours), Warrant 3 (vehicle peak hour), and Warrant 4 (pedestrian
  peak hour). The number of reported collisions for each location also did not meet Warrant 7
  (crash experience) thresholds. The warrants that assessed the side street traffic volumes
  utilized all right turn traffic. Typically, the right turn traffic is either reduced or removed from
  the traffic signal warrant analyses since right turn traffic from the side street generally can turn
  right within the gaps of traffic on the major street (Pacific Boulevard). Even with this
  conservative approach, the side street traffic volumes did not meet any of the traffic signal
  warrant criteria.

In addition to above (A) and (B) findings, at the intersection of 49th Street, there is very low pedestrian
demand crossing on Pacific Boulevard and the crosswalk is located approximately only 320 feet from
the crosswalk at Leonis Boulevard. Then to enhance pedestrian safety, the crosswalk at 49th Street
could be removed since a controlled crossing is available at Leonis Boulevard for pedestrians to cross
Pacific Boulevard.

The intersection of 45th Street and Pacific Boulevard has existing pedestrian crossing signs at both
advanced approaches and at the intersection along Pacific Boulevard. Although this signing is not
required based on the posted speed on Pacific Boulevard (not greater than 40 mph), the City could
install the same signs at 46th and 49th street for both northbound and southbound approaches.

Subject
Consulting Services Agreement with CNS Engineers, Inc. for the Atlantic Boulevard Bridge
Rehabilitation and Widening Project

Recommendation
A. Find that the proposed action is within the Initial Study/Mitigated Negative Declaration
prepared for this project pursuant to the provisions under the California Environmental Quality
Act (CEQA) in accordance with Section 15063 of the CEQA Guidelines;
B. Find that the best interests of the City are served by a direct award of a Services Agreement
to CNS Engineers, Inc., without a competitive selection process pursuant to Vernon Municipal
Code Section 3.32.110 (B)(2); and
C. Approve and authorize the City Administrator to execute a Services Agreement with CNS
Engineers, Inc. for the rehabilitation and widening of the Atlantic Boulevard Bridge (Federal
Project No. DBPL02-5139(010)).

Background
The Atlantic Boulevard Bridge, originally constructed in 1931, is a vital regional corridor that
currently carries over 50,000 vehicles daily. Due to its age and narrow pedestrian and vehicular
lanes, the bridge no longer meets modern traffic demands. In November 2009, the City awarded
a design and right-of-way support agreement to CNS Engineers, Inc. via Resolution No. 10,112.
While the design and right-of-way phase is nearing completion, the project has experienced
delays due to the complexities of coordinating with multiple external agencies. These external
entities, including the BNSF Railway Company (BNSF), the Los Angeles Department of Water
and Power (LADWP), and the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans), each have
independent requirements and review timelines that have exceeded the project’s original
schedule.

The proposed new agreement will provide an extension and additional funding to allow CNS to:
(1) finalize the escrow and recording of easements for the LADWP and Magellan Atlantic
properties; (2) execute the BNSF Railroad Construction and Management (C&M) Agreement and
obtain California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) construction permits; (3) finalize relocation
plans with Southern California Edison (SCE) and Maywood Mutual Water Company #3; and (4)
secure final Right-of-Way Certification and construction authorization from Caltrans.

City Attorney’s office recommended executing a new agreement since the original agreement
has been in place since 2009, and the City has an updated agreement template. To remain
compliant with Caltrans Local Assistance requirements, the new agreement must be approved
before the expiration of Contract No. CS-0099. Therefore, pursuant to Vernon Municipal Code
(VMC) Section 3.32.110(B)(2), it is in the best interest of the City to enter into a new agreement
with CNS to finalize the design phase of the bridge widening project as this will allow for continuity
of services and for the City to remain in compliance with Caltrans Local Assistance requirements.

Pursuant to VMC Section 3.32.030(A), City Council approval is required for contracts with a total

Dear Mr. Wall:

To complete the proposed project in PE Phase, we request an amendment for extra work as follows:

1. Extend the Professional Service Agreement (PSA) from December 31, 2025, to December 31, 2028:

  CNS’s PSA will expire on December 31, 2025. The project has completed the design; however, there
  are several pending items listed below to be continuously coordinated and completed before the
  project is certified by Caltrans and ready for construction advertising:

    Continue coordination to close acquisition escrow and record easements for the impacted
  LADWP properties (6304-007-274 and 6314-033-271). Per discussion with LADPW, possession
  of a temporary user agreement for both street permanent easement and temporary construction
  easement will be obtained for Caltrans right-of-way certification while a license agreement will
  be processed through the Board, which may take a while.
    Finalize acquisition and record the easements in the Magellan Atlantic property (APN 6314-033
  and 005). A temporary user agreement is in possession for Caltrans’ right-of-way certification.
  The property owner requests updating the older appraisal, and subsequently the acquisition will
  be finalized, and the escrow will be closed.
    Continue coordination to execute the BNSF Railroad Construction and Management (C&M)
  Agreement that addresses all railroad-related costs. Approval of the design is expected in March
  2026, and the C&M Agreement will be materialized. No more major comments are expected.
    Obtain the CPUC GO 88B Construction Permit. Additional minor CPUC comments will be
  addressed. No more major comments are expected.
    Continue coordinating with the City and SCE to obtain utility design permits from BNSF. The
  permits are for the temporary electric overhead shoofly and the permanent electric underground
  casings across the at-grade rail crossings, which were prepared by the City’s electric consultant
  (Petrelli Electric). The two permitting applications have been submitted for review by BNSF.
    Continue obtaining a conditional encroachment permit from Caltrans District 7 for traffic controls
  at the I-710/Bandini Interchange involving a 4-day street closure in two weekends to replace the
  rail crossings adjacent to the bridge.
    Coordinate with neighboring cities (Maywood, Bell and Commerce) as needed for approval of
  traffic control plans.
    Complete utility relocation coordination involving the City, SCE and Maywood Mutual Water
  Company #3.
    Obtain the Right of Way Certification from Caltrans.
    Extend ACOE 408 and 404 Permits.
    Assist the City in obtaining Construction Authorization from Caltrans.

  Regular City Council Meeting Minutes  Page 2 of 7
  March 17, 2026

  PRESENTATIONS

  1.  Employee Service Pin Awards
  Recommendation: Recognize February 2026 Employee Service Pin Award
  recipient.

  Human Resources Director Tan presented the staff report, and City Council
  recognized the February 2026 Employee Service Pin Award Recipient: Facilities
  Maintenance Worker, Richard A. Cimarusti.

  2.  City Council Strategic Priorities
  Recommendation: Receive a presentation on potential City Council goals and
  determine key goals to guide the City’s strategic planning process.

  City Administrator Saeki presented the staff report and accompanying PowerPoint
  presentation.

  Discussion ensued regarding publicizing the goals and achievements on the City’s
  website.

  City Administrator confirmed the information would be made public facing on the
  website and available on social media.

  Mayor Lopez invited public comment and further discussion from Council. There
  being none, Mayor Lopez initiated a motion.

  MOTION
  Mayor Lopez moved and Council Member Rivera seconded a motion to approve
  the highlighted goals to formulate a strategic plan. The question was called and
  the motion carried unanimously.

  PUBLIC HEARINGS

  3.  Adoption of the 2025 California Building Standards Code by Reference
  Recommendation: A. Conduct a Public Hearing; B. Find that the proposed action
  is exempt from California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) review, because it is
  general policy and procedure-making activity that is unrelated to any specific
  project, which must undergo separate CEQA review, and that will not result in direct
  physical changes or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical changes in the
  environment, and therefore does not constitute a “project” as defined by CEQA
  Guidelines Section 15378; and C. Adopt Ordinance No. 1310 adopting the 2025
  California Building Standards Code by reference.

  Public Works Director Wall presented the staff report.
 Docusign Envelope ID: DF104054-2B58-473F-B79B-AC1FA8AE0F37

  Regular City Council Meeting Minutes  Page 3 of 7
  March 17, 2026

  Mayor Lopez opened the public hearing at 9:24 a.m. There being no speakers,
  Mayor Lopez closed the public hearing at 9:24 a.m.

  Mayor Lopez invited further Council questions. There being none, Mayor Lopez
  called for a motion.

  MOTION
  Mayor Pro Tem Ybarra moved and Mayor Lopez seconded a motion to approve
  recommendations A, B, and C. The question was called and the motion carried
  unanimously.

  4.  Sidewalk Vending Regulations
  Recommendation: A. Conduct a Public Hearing; B. Find that the proposed action
  is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to CEQA
  Guidelines Sections 15061(b)(3) and 15378, as an action for which there is no
  possibility that the ordinance will have any significant effect on the environment; C.
  Introduce, read by title only, and waive further reading of Ordinance No. 1311
  amending Chapter 12.10 (Sidewalk Vending) of Title 12 (Streets, Sidewalks and
  Public Places) of the Vernon Municipal Code pertaining to the regulation of
  sidewalk vending; and D. Direct staff to schedule the adoption for the April 7, 2026,
  City Council meeting.

  Public Works Director Wall presented the staff report.

  Mayor Lopez opened the public hearing at 9:26 a.m. There being no speakers,
  Mayor Lopez closed the public hearing at 9:26 a.m.

  Mayor Lopez invited further Council questions. There being none, Mayor Lopez
  called for a motion.

  City Clerk Rocha read the title to Ordinance No. 1311

  MOTION
  Council Member Larios moved and Council Member Merlo seconded a motion to
  approve recommendations A, B, C, and D. The question was called and the motion
  carried unanimously.

  CONSENT CALENDAR

  Mayor Lopez invited public comments. There being none, Mayor Lopez, called for
  a motion.

  MOTION
  Council Member Rivera moved and Mayor Pro Tem Ybarra seconded a motion to
  approve the Consent Calendar. The question was called and the motion carried
  unanimously.

  The Consent Calendar consisted of the following items:
  5.  Meeting Minutes
  Recommendation: Approve the March 3, 2026 Regular City Council and Special
  City Council Meeting Minutes.
  6.  Operating Account Warrant Register
  Recommendation: Approve Operating Account Warrant Register No. 169, for the
  period of February 1, 2026 through February 14, 2026, totaling $9,191,307.17 and
  consisting of ratification of electronic payments totaling $8,795,879.66 and
  ratification of the issuance of early checks totaling $395,427.51.
  7.  Fire Department Activity Report
  Recommendation: Receive and file the January 2026 Fire Department Activity
  Report.
  8.  Police Department Activity Report - January 2026
  Recommendation: Receive and file the January 2026 Police Department Activity
  Report.
  9.  Professional Services Agreement with Actum-E, LLC
  Recommendation: A. Find that it is in the best interests of the City to award a
  contract directly to Actum-E, LLC without a competitive selection process, pursuant
  to Vernon Municipal Code Section 3.32.110(B)(2); and B. Approve and authorize
  the City Administrator to execute a Professional Services Agreement with Actum-
  E, LLC, in substantially the same form as submitted, for government affairs related
  to the Big 4 cities, for a total amount not-to-exceed $45,000, through June 30,
  2026.
  10.  Amendment No. 1 to Attorney Services Agreement with Liebert Cassidy
  Whitmore
  Recommendation: Approve and authorize the City Administrator to execute
  Amendment No. 1 to the Attorney Services Agreement with Liebert Cassidy
  Whitmore (LCW) for outside legal services, in substantially the same form as
  submitted, to increase the total not-to-exceed amount by an additional $75,000.
  11.  Side Letters of Agreement with Police Bargaining Groups Regarding In-Lieu
  Holiday Time
  Recommendation: A. Adopt Resolution No. 2026-011 approving the In-Lieu
  Holiday Time Side Letter of Agreement by and between the City of Vernon and the
  Vernon Police Officers' Benefit Association (VPOBA); and B. Adopt Resolution No.
  2026-012 approving the In-Lieu Holiday Time Side Letter of Agreement by and
  between the City of Vernon and the Vernon Police Management Association
  (VPMA).

  12.  Removal of Marked Crosswalks Along Pacific Boulevard at 45th, 46th, and
  49th Street
  Recommendation: A. Find that the proposed action is categorically exempt from
  California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) review, in accordance with CEQA
  Guidelines Section 15301, because the project consists of restriping an existing
  street by removing the crosswalk markings to avoid potential adverse impacts to
  pedestrian and vehicular safety, and involves negligible or no expansion of an
  existing use; and B. Authorize pavement striping crew to remove all marked
  crosswalks along Pacific Boulevard at 45th, 46th, and 49th Street.

  NEW BUSINESS

  13.  Consulting Services Agreement with CNS Engineers, Inc. for the Atlantic
  Boulevard Bridge Rehabilitation and Widening Project
  Recommendation: A. Find that the proposed action is within the Initial
  Study/Mitigated Negative Declaration prepared for this project pursuant to the
  provisions under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) in accordance
  with Section 15063 of the CEQA Guidelines; B. Find that the best interests of the
  City are served by a direct award of a Services Agreement to CNS Engineers, Inc.,
  without a competitive selection process pursuant to Vernon Municipal Code
  Section 3.32.110 (B)(2); and C. Approve and authorize the City Administrator to
  execute a Services Agreement with CNS Engineers, Inc. for the rehabilitation and
  widening of the Atlantic Boulevard Bridge (Federal Project No. DBPL02-5139(010).

  Public Works Director Wall presented the staff report.

  Mayor Lopez invited public comments. There being none, Mayor Lopez called for
  a motion

  MOTION
  Mayor Pro Tem Ybarra moved and Council Member Merlo seconded a motion to
  approve recommendations A, B, and C. The question was called and the motion
  carried unanimously.

  ORAL REPORTS

  14.  City Administrator Reports on Activities and Other Announcements

  City Administrator Saeki wished everyone a happy St. Patrick’s Day and
  announced the Green Vernon Commission would meet on March 18 at 3:30 pm to
  discuss its work plan and budget for this fiscal year.

  On election related matters, he announced the first day for mailing vote-by-mail
  ballots was Monday, March 16, the last day to register to vote would be Monday,
  March 30, the write-in candidate filing period runs through Wednesday, April 1, he
  reminded the public Election Day would be Tuesday, April 14, 2026, and instructed
 Docusign Envelope ID: DF104054-2B58-473F-B79B-AC1FA8AE0F37

  anyone with questions could reach out to the City Clerk’s Office at
  cityclerk@cityofvernonca.gov.

  Regarding the Vernon CommUNITY Fund Scholarships, he announced a reminder
  that scholarship applications would be due Thursday, March 26th. Students may
  submit their applications via email or deliver them to City Hall. More information
  could be found on the City’s website cityofvernonca.gov/communityfund.

  He announced the annual Spring Egg-Stravaganza event would be scheduled for
  Thursday, March 26 from 5:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. TK Burgers would be serving
  dinner while families could enjoy fun activities, raffle prizes and an egg hunt.

  Lastly, he announced heat advisories would be in effect through 8:00 p.m., Friday
  March 20th. Cooling centers throughout Los Angeles County could be found by
  accessing a link on the City’s community resources webpage.

  Directives to Staff

  None.
